messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Ministry Worker
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 47

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the office with his hands folded in his lap, a habit he's developed over the past eighteen months. He's a young man who looks older than twenty-one—there's a weariness in how he holds himself, a carefulness in his movements. His wedding ring catches the light as he shifts in his seat. He and his wife Elena got married just before he left for the humanitarian mission, a decision that now feels like it belonged to a different version of himself.

Two years ago, Marcus was working as a social ministry worker in his home country, helping vulnerable families access resources and support. When a major conflict erupted in a neighboring region, his organization asked for volunteers to establish aid distribution centers in affected areas. Marcus felt called to go. He was young, unmarried at the time, and believed he could make a tangible difference. Elena, his girlfriend then, supported the decision, though she worried. They married quickly before he deployed, wanting that commitment before he left.

The first month was intense but manageable. Marcus helped coordinate food and medical supply distribution, worked with displaced families, and documented needs for his organization. He felt purposeful. Then came the day that everything fractured. A market where he'd been working that morning was hit by an airstrike in the afternoon. Marcus wasn't there—he'd left an hour before it happened. But he knew people who were there. He spent the next hours searching through rubble, helping pull bodies out, holding dying people's hands because they had no one else. He can still smell it, still see the faces. He doesn't talk about the specific details, but his body remembers.

Marcus finished his deployment, returned home after four months, and tried to resume his life. But the world had become a different place. He startles at loud noises—car backfires send him into a state of panic that takes hours to settle. He's hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. When he's driving, he finds himself scanning rooftops and calculating escape routes, habits that served him in the conflict zone but make no sense on suburban streets. He knows this intellectually, but his body doesn't believe him.

Sleep has become a nightly negotiation. Most nights he lies awake beside Elena, afraid of the nightmares that come when he finally drifts off. In the dreams, he's back in the rubble, but this time the faces are people he loves—Elena, his parents, his colleagues. He wakes gasping, disoriented, sometimes aggressive in his confusion. Elena has learned not to touch him when he wakes. They've learned a lot of things about managing around his trauma.

His work as a social ministry worker continues, but it's different now. He returned to his position, wanting to help again, but he finds himself emotionally numb with clients. He goes through the motions competently—he's good at his job, people tell him so—but he can't access the genuine compassion he once felt. When families share their struggles, he hears them as if through glass. Part of him judges himself harshly for this distance. Another part of him is terrified of opening that door again, of feeling too much.

Elena notices everything. She notices when he's irritable with her for no reason, when he withdraws into himself for days, when he drinks more than he used to. She's trying to be patient, but Marcus can feel the strain. He loves her, but he's not sure he knows how to be present with her anymore. There's a part of him that feels permanently altered, and he's not certain that part can be repaired.
